title: How LLMs Work
tagline: Large language models predict the next token — and from that single objective, language understanding emerges.

sections.content:
In late 2022, a chatbot answered a coding question, wrote a sonnet, and debugged a Python script in the same conversation — and the world took notice. Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-4, Claude, and Gemini are the technology behind this shift. But what are they, actually? The honest one-sentence answer is: **a neural network trained to predict the next token in a sequence of text.** That is it. The magic — the apparent reasoning, creativity, and knowledge — emerges from doing that one thing at extraordinary scale, on nearly all the text humanity has ever written.

Understanding LLMs is no longer academic. If you write software today, you will call an LLM API, evaluate model responses, manage context windows, or debug a prompt that stopped working. The engineers who build reliable LLM-powered systems understand the mechanics: tokens, embeddings, the Transformer architecture, training dynamics, and inference behaviour. Without that foundation, you are flying blind.

This chapter builds that foundation systematically. We will walk through **six core concepts**: (1) tokenisation — how text becomes integers; (2) embeddings — how integers become geometry; (3) the Transformer — how context is processed via attention; (4) training — how weights are learned from trillions of tokens; (5) inference — how frozen weights generate new text; and (6) alignment — how raw prediction becomes a helpful assistant. Along the way we will look at real code, work through the attention formula by hand, and examine the edge cases that trip up practitioners.

A brief orientation: LLMs have a **knowledge cutoff** (they do not know events after their training data), they can **hallucinate** (state false information confidently), and they are **stateless** between API calls (the illusion of memory is just a long context). These are not bugs to be fixed with better prompting — they are direct consequences of the architecture we are about to explore.

    B --> C["Token IDs\n[1923, 318, 257, ...]"]

sections.title: An Extraordinarily Well-Read Autocomplete
sections.content:
Your phone's keyboard suggests the next word as you type. An LLM is conceptually the same mechanism — but trained on essentially the entire internet rather than your personal messages, with 70 billion learned parameters instead of a simple frequency table, and looking at thousands of prior tokens instead of the last two or three words.

The analogy also reveals the key limitation: your phone's autocomplete does not 'understand' your message — it learned statistical patterns over text. LLMs do the same thing at a scale where those patterns become indistinguishable from understanding, at least for many practical tasks. When a model correctly explains why a recursive function causes a stack overflow, it is not reasoning from first principles the way you are — it is pattern-matching against millions of similar explanations in its training data.

The critical architectural difference between phone autocomplete and LLMs is **attention**: autocomplete looks at a fixed short window of recent words. An LLM's self-attention mechanism looks at **every single token in the context simultaneously**, weighting each one's relevance. When completing 'The Eiffel Tower is located in the city of...', attention routes focus toward 'Eiffel Tower' even if hundreds of unrelated tokens separate the phrase from the blank — because the attention weights learned that those three tokens together predict 'Paris' with high probability. That global, parallel, learned relevance weighting is what makes LLMs qualitatively different from everything that came before.

sections.title: Tokenisation: How Text Becomes Numbers
sections.content:
Before any neural network can process text, the text must become numbers. **Tokens** are the atomic units that an LLM sees — neither characters nor words, but something in between.

The most common algorithm is **Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE)**, invented in 1994 for data compression and adapted for NLP in 2016. BPE starts from individual characters (or bytes) and repeatedly merges the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token, stopping when the vocabulary reaches a target size. GPT-4o uses approximately 100,000 tokens; Llama 3 uses 128,000. The result: very common words like 'the' or 'is' are a single token; rarer words like 'tokenisation' split into subwords like `['token', 'isation']`; completely unseen words split into small subword pieces or individual bytes.

This matters practically for several reasons. First, **token count determines cost**: every API call bills by input and output tokens. Second, **token count determines speed**: each new token requires a full forward pass through the model. Third, **different languages tokenise differently**: English is ~0.75 words per token; Japanese or Chinese text can tokenise much less efficiently because those languages were underrepresented in training data and thus fewer characters have dedicated tokens.

A worked example: the string `'Hello, world!'` tokenises to `[9906, 11, 1917, 0]` in GPT-4o (4 tokens). `'antidisestablishmentarianism'` tokenises to `['ant', 'idis', 'establishment', 'arian', 'ism']` — 5 tokens. `'1234567890'` might be 3-5 tokens depending on the tokeniser. Code often tokenises poorly because many identifier names are rare.

**Token IDs are just integers** — indices into the vocabulary table. The integer `9906` does not mean 'Hello'; it means 'row 9906 in our embedding matrix'. Meaning is not in the integer — it is in the embedding vector that integer indexes.

flowchart TD
    A["Raw string: unhappiness"] --> B["BPE split"]
    B --> C["un | happ | iness"]
    C --> D["Token IDs: [348, 71, 2083]"]
    D --> E["Embedding lookup"]

sections.caption: BPE tokenisation splits an unknown word into known subword pieces. Each piece becomes an integer ID, which indexes into the embedding matrix to produce a dense vector.

sections.title: Embeddings: How Numbers Become Geometry
sections.content:
A token ID like `9906` is just a row number. To give it meaning, the model looks up a row in the **embedding matrix** — a learned table of shape `(vocab_size, d_model)`. For a model with 100,000 vocabulary tokens and a hidden dimension of 4,096 (like LLaMA 3 8B), the embedding matrix has 400 million numbers — about 1.6 GB at float32.

The resulting vector is a point in high-dimensional space. The remarkable property — not hard-coded, but **learned during training** — is that semantically similar tokens end up geometrically close. 'king', 'queen', 'monarch', 'ruler' cluster near each other. 'Paris', 'London', 'Tokyo' cluster near each other. The famous example from Word2Vec: `embedding('king') - embedding('man') + embedding('woman') ≈ embedding('queen')`. Arithmetic on vectors corresponds to semantic relationships.

But token embeddings alone have no positional information. The word 'dog' has the same embedding whether it appears first or last in a sentence — and yet position matters enormously for meaning. To fix this, **positional encodings** are added to each token's embedding. The original Transformer paper used fixed sinusoidal functions of position; modern models (including LLaMA, GPT-4) use **Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE)** or **Absolute Learned Positional Embeddings (APE)** — different schemes with different trade-offs for long contexts.

The combination — token embedding plus positional encoding — is the input to the first Transformer layer. After this point, the model works purely in this continuous vector space; it never sees characters or integers again until it produces its final output.

sections.title: The Transformer: Architecture of the Revolution
sections.content:
The Transformer was introduced in the 2017 paper 'Attention Is All You Need' by Vaswani et al. at Google. Before it, the dominant sequence models were RNNs (Recurrent Neural Networks) — networks that process tokens one at a time, maintaining a hidden state. RNNs had two fatal flaws: they could not parallelise (you must finish token 5 before processing token 6), and they struggled to retain information from very early in a long sequence (the **vanishing gradient problem**).

The Transformer abandoned recurrence entirely. It processes all tokens in parallel using **attention** — a mechanism that lets each token directly communicate with every other token regardless of distance. This enables two things: massively parallel training on modern GPU hardware, and perfect memory across the full context window.

A GPT-style (decoder-only) Transformer is a stack of **N identical blocks**. Each block contains two sub-layers:

**1. Multi-Head Self-Attention (MHSA)**: The core operation. Each token computes a query vector `Q`, a key vector `K`, and a value vector `V` via three learned weight matrices. The attention output is:

`Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q Kᵀ / sqrt(d_k)) V`

Intuitively: each token (via its query Q) scans all other tokens (via their keys K) to compute relevance scores. Softmax converts scores to weights that sum to 1. The output is a weighted sum of all tokens' value vectors. Multiple attention heads run in parallel — each head learns to look for different relationship types (syntactic, semantic, coreference, etc.). Heads' outputs are concatenated and projected back to `d_model`.

**Causal masking** is applied during training so that position `i` can only attend to positions `0..i`. This prevents 'cheating' by looking at future tokens, and is what makes the model useful for generation: at inference time, you give it a prefix and it can only use the information it has.

**2. Feed-Forward Network (FFN)**: After attention mixes information across tokens, the FFN processes each token's representation independently through a two-layer MLP with a non-linearity (typically GeLU or SiLU): `FFN(x) = W₂ · activation(W₁x + b₁) + b₂`. The inner dimension is usually 4× the model dimension, giving a large capacity layer. Modern MoE (Mixture of Experts) models replace this dense FFN with sparse expert networks where each token routes to a subset of experts.

**Residual connections and Layer Normalisation** wrap both sub-layers: `output = LayerNorm(x + sublayer(x))`. Residual connections allow gradients to flow directly to early layers, enabling training of very deep networks. Layer norm stabilises activations across training.

A modern large model like GPT-4 reportedly has 128 layers (N=128), a model dimension of 12,288, and 96 attention heads — over a trillion parameters in its Mixture-of-Experts configuration.

flowchart TD
    A["Token Embeddings + Positional Encoding"]
    A --> B["Multi-Head Self-Attention"]
    B --> C["Add and Norm (Residual)"]
    C --> D["Feed-Forward Network (MLP)"]
    D --> E["Add and Norm (Residual)"]
    E --> F["Next Transformer Block (repeat N times)"]
    F --> G["Linear Projection (d_model → vocab_size)"]
    G --> H["Softmax over Vocabulary"]
sections.caption: One Transformer decoder block. After N identical blocks, a linear projection expands hidden states to vocabulary size for the final softmax probability distribution.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The attention computation: Q[0] matches K[0] perfectly (both [1,0]) giving a high dot product. After softmax, 57.6% of the output comes from V[0]. The sqrt(dk) scaling is crucial — without it, dot products grow proportionally to the dimension size, pushing softmax into saturation where all weight collapses on one token and gradients through other positions become zero.

sections.title: Multi-Head Attention: Why Multiple Heads?
sections.content:
A single attention head applies one set of Q, K, V projection matrices — learning one particular 'type' of relevance across the sequence. In practice, a sentence has many simultaneous relationship types: syntactic agreement ('cats' is plural, 'are' must be plural), semantic similarity ('Paris' relates to 'city'), coreference ('she' refers to 'Alice'), and more.

**Multi-head attention** runs `h` attention heads in parallel, each with its own learned Q, K, V projections of dimension `d_k = d_model / h`. The outputs of all heads are concatenated and projected back to `d_model` via a final weight matrix `W_O`. The cost is the same as one head with dimension `d_model` (because `h × d_k = d_model`), but the model can simultaneously attend to different subspaces.

Analysis of trained models shows this is not just theoretical: different heads do specialise. In language models, some heads track syntactic structure, others handle long-range coreferences, others handle local collocations. The multi-head structure is a key reason why Transformers handle diverse linguistic phenomena better than any single attention pattern could.

For the numbers: LLaMA 3 8B uses `h=32` heads with `d_model=4096`, so each head operates in `d_k=128` dimensions. GPT-4 reportedly uses `h=96` heads with `d_model=12288`, giving `d_k=128` per head as well — suggesting 128 is empirically a good per-head dimension.

sections.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A["Input x (d_model)"] --> B["Head 1\nQ1,K1,V1"]
    A --> C["Head 2\nQ2,K2,V2"]
    A --> D["Head h\nQh,Kh,Vh"]
    B --> E["Concat"]
    C --> E
    D --> E
    E --> F["W_O projection"]
    F --> G["Output (d_model)"]
sections.caption: Multi-head attention: h parallel heads each with dimension d_k = d_model/h. Outputs are concatenated and reprojected, keeping the total dimensionality constant.

sections.title: Training: Learning from the Entire Internet
sections.content:
How do you teach a model to do all of this? Through **next-token prediction** on an enormous corpus, and nothing else. The training objective is deceptively simple:

Given tokens `t₁, t₂, ..., tₙ`, the model predicts `tₙ₊₁`. Loss = cross-entropy between predicted distribution and the true next token. Summed over billions of positions. Gradients computed via backpropagation. Weights updated via the Adam optimiser. Repeat for months.

**The scale of training** is staggering. GPT-3 was trained on 300 billion tokens. LLaMA 3 70B was trained on 15 trillion tokens. Each forward pass on a batch of sequences costs billions of multiply-add operations; each backward pass costs roughly twice that. Training GPT-4 reportedly cost over $100 million in compute. This is done once (or a few times for different versions) — the same weights then serve millions of users.

**Why does next-token prediction produce intelligence?** Because accurate prediction requires understanding everything: grammar (wrong grammar makes unlikely next tokens), facts (wrong facts make unlikely continuations), logic (wrong reasoning makes non sequitur continuations), and even emotional tone. The model that best predicts text is implicitly the model that best models the world that produced the text. This is the key insight: **the training objective is a proxy for world modelling**.

**Pre-training vs. fine-tuning**: The process above is **pre-training** — training on raw internet text. The result is a **base model** that is good at predicting text but does not follow instructions, refuses nothing, and may produce harmful content. Fine-tuning adapts the base model for specific applications:

- **Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT)**: Show the model examples of (instruction, ideal response) pairs. Train with the same next-token loss but only on the response portion. This teaches instruction following.
- **RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback)**: Human raters compare pairs of model outputs and rank them. A separate **reward model** is trained to predict human preference scores. The LLM is then fine-tuned using PPO (Proximal Policy Optimisation) to maximise reward model scores — making it more helpful, honest, and harmless. This is what turns a base LLM into ChatGPT or Claude.
- **DPO (Direct Preference Optimisation)**: A simpler alternative to RLHF that directly optimises on preference pairs without training a separate reward model. Increasingly preferred for its stability.

**Emergent capabilities** are abilities that appear at scale without explicit training. Below a certain parameter count, models cannot reliably do chain-of-thought reasoning or multi-step arithmetic. Above it, the capability appears, seemingly spontaneously. This has led to debate about whether capability jumps are truly emergent or just artefacts of how we measure performance.

sections.title: Inference: Generating Text Token by Token
sections.content:
Once training is complete, the model's weights are **frozen**. Inference is how the frozen model generates new text.

When you send a message to an LLM API, the following happens:

1. **Tokenise the prompt**: Your text is converted to a sequence of token IDs.
2. **Prefill (parallel forward pass)**: All prompt tokens are processed simultaneously in a single forward pass through all N Transformer layers. This produces the KV tensors for every prompt token and the logits for the last position. This step is compute-bound.
3. **Decode (autoregressive generation)**: Using the logits from the last position, sample or select the next token. Append it to the sequence. Run another forward pass — but now the KV-cache means you only compute the new token's Q, K, V and attend to cached K, V from all previous tokens. This step is memory-bandwidth-bound.
4. **Repeat** until `<EOS>` (end-of-sequence) token or max length.

**The KV-cache** is the critical optimisation that makes inference tractable. Without it, generating token `n` would require recomputing attention over all `n-1` previous tokens from scratch — `O(n²)` work per new token. With the KV-cache, you cache the K and V matrices from all previous tokens in GPU memory and only compute the new token's contribution. This reduces each decode step to approximately `O(n)` memory reads (to load the cached K and V). The trade-off: large KV-caches consume enormous GPU memory, which limits how many requests can run concurrently (batch size).

**Sampling strategies** control how a token is chosen from the logit distribution:
- **Greedy**: always pick the highest-probability token. Deterministic but often repetitive.
- **Temperature sampling**: divide logits by temperature `T` before softmax. `T < 1` sharpens the distribution (more deterministic); `T > 1` flattens it (more random). `T = 0` approaches greedy.
- **Top-k sampling**: restrict sampling to the k highest-probability tokens. Cuts off the long tail of low-probability choices.
- **Top-p (nucleus) sampling**: sample from the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds `p`. Adapts the number of candidates to the distribution's shape.
- **Beam search**: maintain the top-B sequences in parallel, selecting the globally highest-probability full sequence. Used in translation; rarely in chat models (too repetitive).

Most production LLM APIs default to some combination of temperature + top-p sampling. The exact combination dramatically affects output quality and style.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Temperature controls the sharpness of the probability distribution before sampling. At T=0 the highest-probability token is always chosen (greedy). As T increases, lower-probability tokens become more likely, introducing variety. Top-p sampling (nucleus sampling) adapts the candidate set size dynamically — rather than always sampling from the top-k tokens, it takes the smallest set of tokens that covers p% of the probability mass, which naturally takes more tokens when the model is uncertain and fewer when it is confident.

sections.title: The Context Window: Working Memory with a Hard Limit
sections.content:
The **context window** is the maximum number of tokens the model can process in a single forward pass. Everything inside the context window is equally accessible to the model — attention can connect any two positions. Everything outside is completely invisible.

Context lengths have grown dramatically: the original GPT-2 had 1,024 tokens; GPT-4o has 128,000; Claude 3.5 Sonnet has 200,000; Gemini 1.5 Pro has 1,000,000. Each jump required engineering effort because the naive attention algorithm scales as `O(n²)` in both compute and memory — doubling context length quadruples the attention cost.

Solutions for long contexts include:
- **FlashAttention**: A hardware-aware algorithm that tiles the attention computation to avoid materialising the full `n×n` attention matrix in GPU SRAM. Same mathematical output, but orders-of-magnitude less memory and significantly faster.
- **Sliding window attention**: Each token attends only to a local window of positions rather than the full context. Used in Longformer and some Mistral variants. Breaks the `O(n²)` cost at the expense of not having global attention.
- **Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)**: Multiple query heads share a single key-value head, reducing the KV-cache size. Used in LLaMA 3 and Mistral.
- **RoPE positional encoding**: By applying positional information directly to the Q and K vectors during attention (rather than to the input embeddings), RoPE naturally extrapolates to longer sequences than seen during training.

From an application perspective, the context window is **working memory**. The model cannot remember previous conversations that have scrolled out of the window. This is why chat applications maintain a conversation history buffer, trim it when it grows too large, and sometimes use summarisation to compress older turns. **Prompt caching** (available in the Anthropic and OpenAI APIs) allows the server to cache the KV representations of a repeated system prompt, reducing latency and cost for applications that send the same long system prompt with every request.

sections.title: Hallucination, Uncertainty, and Knowledge Cutoffs
sections.content:
Three limitations of LLMs are direct consequences of the architecture, not implementation flaws:

**Hallucination**: LLMs generate the most probable continuation of a sequence. When the answer to a question is not well-represented in training data, the model still generates text — it just generates plausible-sounding text that may be factually wrong. The model has no mechanism to say 'I don't have this in my training data' and refuse; it will instead pattern-match to something superficially similar. Hallucination is worst for specific facts (exact numbers, dates, names) and improves for well-documented topics.

**Knowledge cutoff**: Training data has a cutoff date. The model has no knowledge of events after that date. GPT-4o has a knowledge cutoff of April 2024; Claude 3.5 Sonnet has a cutoff of April 2024. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is the standard solution: retrieve up-to-date documents at inference time and inject them into the context window, then ask the model to answer using those documents rather than its parametric memory.

**No uncertainty quantification**: Unlike Bayesian models, a standard LLM cannot output calibrated confidence scores. A model that says 'I am 95% confident the answer is X' is not actually measuring its internal certainty — it is generating text that includes a confidence expression. The actual probability distribution over the vocabulary tells you how confident the model is in the *next token*, not in the *claim being made*. This is a fundamental limitation for high-stakes applications like medical diagnosis.

These are not bugs that will be patched — they are properties of the training objective. Understanding them lets you design around them: use RAG for facts, use retrieval for recency, use structured output validation to catch hallucinated formats, and use human review for high-stakes claims.

    B --> C["Vector Search\n(cosine similarity)"]

sections.title: Model Size, Scaling Laws, and Parameter Counts
sections.content:
LLM parameter counts are frequently cited but rarely explained. **Parameters** are the learned floating-point weights — the Q, K, V projection matrices, the FFN weights, the embedding matrix, and the output head. For a decoder-only Transformer, the dominant costs are:

- Embedding matrix: `vocab_size × d_model` (e.g. 128,000 × 4,096 ≈ 500M params for LLaMA 3 8B)
- Per Transformer block: `4 × d_model²` (attention) + `8 × d_model²` (FFN with 4× expansion) ≈ `12 × d_model²`
- For 32 layers: `32 × 12 × 4096² ≈ 6.4B` params
- Plus embedding ≈ 8B total (matching the name)

The **Chinchilla scaling laws** (Hoffmann et al. 2022, DeepMind) established a crucial empirical finding: for a given compute budget, you get better models by training a **smaller model on more tokens** than by training a larger model on fewer tokens. The optimal ratio is roughly 20 tokens per parameter. LLaMA 3 8B, trained on 15 trillion tokens, uses a 1,875× larger token-to-parameter ratio than Chinchilla-optimal — but this produces a model that is cheaper to run (inference cost scales with size) while still achieving excellent performance, because the extra training data keeps improving the model even at overtraining.

The practical implication: model size alone does not determine capability. A well-trained small model can outperform a poorly-trained large model. When evaluating models, look at benchmark results on your task type, not just parameter counts.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The parameter estimate shows where the numbers actually come from. For LLaMA 3 8B, the embedding matrix alone is ~500M parameters — a large fraction. Each Transformer block adds ~200M. The Chinchilla calculation reveals why LLaMA trains for far more tokens than 'optimal': an overtrained smaller model is cheaper to run at inference time (lower latency, lower memory) while matching a larger model trained optimally.

sections.content: **A brief history:** The Transformer architecture was published in June 2017 ('Attention Is All You Need', Vaswani et al.). BERT (2018, Google) showed bidirectional Transformers excel at understanding. GPT-1 (2018, OpenAI) showed decoder-only Transformers work for generation. GPT-2 (2019) was initially withheld due to concerns about misuse — 1.5B parameters seemed enormous at the time. GPT-3 (2020, 175B parameters) demonstrated dramatic few-shot capabilities. InstructGPT (2022) added RLHF, producing the first instruction-following models. ChatGPT launched November 2022 using the InstructGPT approach and reached 100 million users in two months. GPT-4 (2023) introduced multimodality; Claude 2 and 3 extended context windows; Llama 2 and 3 (Meta) made large open-weight models widely available. The entire field moved from research curiosity to mainstream infrastructure in under five years.

**Common misconceptions to clear up before interviews or production work:**

**'LLMs know the answer and are hiding it.'** No — the model generates the most probable continuation. There is no hidden 'real answer' being suppressed. If it gives a wrong answer confidently, it means wrong-but-plausible text had high probability given training data.

**'Temperature 0 is deterministic.'** Almost: `temperature=0` means greedy decoding, but some APIs still apply stochastic operations (dropout, etc.) at inference or use approximate arithmetic that introduces variance. Never rely on bit-for-bit reproducibility unless the API explicitly guarantees it.

**'More context is always better.'** Performance on tasks within the context window can degrade in very long contexts — the so-called 'lost in the middle' phenomenon where models attend poorly to content in the middle of very long inputs. For retrieval tasks, smaller well-curated context can outperform massive raw context.

**'A bigger model is always better.'** Chinchilla showed training data quality and quantity matter as much as model size. A well-tuned 7B model can beat a poorly-tuned 70B model on specific tasks. Always benchmark on your actual use case.

**'LLMs are looking things up.'** Base LLMs have no access to external tools or databases during inference — knowledge is baked into weights at training time. When you see a model 'search the web', that is an **external tool call** added by the application layer, not native model capability.

items: **Tokens** are subword text units produced by BPE tokenisation (~0.75 English words per token). Token count determines API cost, generation speed, and whether content fits in the context window. Token efficiency varies significantly across languages.

**Embeddings** map token IDs to dense vectors in a high-dimensional space where semantic similarity is encoded as geometric proximity. Positional encodings are added to give the model knowledge of token order, since self-attention is inherently position-agnostic.

**Self-attention** — `softmax(QKᵀ/sqrt(dk))V` — allows every token to attend to every other token in the context simultaneously. Multiple parallel heads specialise in different relationship types. The `sqrt(dk)` scaling prevents softmax saturation and gradient vanishing.

**Training** runs next-token prediction on trillions of tokens using cross-entropy loss and Adam optimisation. This single objective implicitly requires the model to learn grammar, facts, reasoning, and world knowledge. Fine-tuning (SFT) and alignment (RLHF/DPO) then make the base model useful and safe.

**Inference** tokenises the prompt, runs a parallel prefill forward pass, then generates tokens autoregressively one at a time. The KV-cache avoids recomputing previous tokens' Key/Value matrices, making generation practical. Temperature and top-p sampling control output randomness.

**Hallucination and knowledge cutoffs** are fundamental architectural properties, not bugs. RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is the standard mitigation: retrieve relevant, current documents and inject them into the context for the model to reason over.

**Scaling laws** (Chinchilla) show that compute budget is best spent on a smaller model trained on more tokens. Model size alone does not predict capability — training data quality, fine-tuning, and alignment all matter substantially.

quiz.question: What is the primary training objective of a GPT-style large language model?
options: Classifying whether a sentence is grammatically correct
Predicting the next token given all previous tokens in the sequence
Translating text between different natural languages
Ranking documents by relevance to a query
quiz.explanation: GPT-style models are trained with a causal language modelling objective: given all previous tokens in a sequence, predict the next token. Cross-entropy loss penalises wrong predictions and gradients flow back to update weights. This single objective applied at enormous scale causes broad language understanding to emerge as a side-effect of learning to predict text accurately.

quiz.question: What is Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) and why is it used for tokenisation?
options: A compression algorithm that encodes each byte as a pair of bits
A tokenisation method that iteratively merges the most frequent adjacent character pairs to build a subword vocabulary
A technique that maps each word to exactly one token regardless of frequency
A way to convert text into floating-point vectors for the embedding layer
quiz.explanation: BPE starts from individual characters (or bytes) and repeatedly merges the most frequently adjacent pair into a new vocabulary entry, until the target vocabulary size is reached. This produces a vocabulary where common words are single tokens and rare words decompose into known subword pieces, balancing vocabulary size against coverage of any input text without out-of-vocabulary errors.

quiz.question: In the attention formula `softmax(QKᵀ / sqrt(dk)) V`, what is the purpose of dividing by `sqrt(dk)`?
options: To normalise the attention weights so they sum to 1 across all heads
To prevent dot products from growing large with high-dimensional keys, which would push softmax into saturation and cause vanishing gradients
To convert raw logits into probability scores over the vocabulary
To apply positional information to the attention computation
quiz.explanation: For large dk, dot products of random Q and K vectors grow in magnitude proportionally to sqrt(dk). Without scaling, large dot products push softmax toward a near-one-hot distribution, where essentially all weight collapses onto one token. This means gradients through all other attention positions vanish nearly to zero, severely hampering training. Dividing by sqrt(dk) keeps dot products in a stable range where softmax gradients remain healthy across all positions.

quiz.question: What does the KV-cache do during LLM inference, and why is it important?
options: It stores the vocabulary embeddings in fast memory to speed up tokenisation
It caches Key and Value matrices from previously processed tokens so they do not need to be recomputed on each new generation step
It is a database of common knowledge injected into the model at startup
It stores conversation history between separate API calls to maintain state
quiz.explanation: During autoregressive generation, each new token requires attention over all previous tokens. Without caching, all K and V matrices would be recomputed from scratch at every step — O(n²) work per new token. The KV-cache saves the K and V tensors from all previous positions in GPU memory. Each new decode step only computes the new token's K and V, then reads from the cache for all others. This is what makes generation fast enough to be practical.

quiz.question: What is the 'context window' of an LLM, and what happens to content that exceeds it?
options: A sliding window that stores the most recent 10 conversation turns between API calls
The maximum number of tokens the model can process in one forward pass; content beyond it is completely invisible to the model
The number of attention heads multiplied by the head dimension
The temperature range applied during sampling to control output randomness
quiz.explanation: The context window is the hard upper bound on tokens per inference call. The model's attention mechanism can connect any two positions within this window — but positions outside it do not exist from the model's perspective. Exceeding the limit requires truncating context, summarising older content, or using RAG to retrieve only the most relevant chunks. GPT-4o supports 128k tokens; Claude 3.5 Sonnet supports 200k; Gemini 1.5 Pro supports 1 million.

quiz.question: What is the difference between pre-training and RLHF fine-tuning in the LLM pipeline?
options: Pre-training uses attention; RLHF does not use attention
Pre-training trains weights on next-token prediction over massive text corpora; RLHF fine-tunes the model using human preference rankings to make it helpful, honest, and harmless
RLHF happens before pre-training to initialise the model's weights
Pre-training is done on GPU; RLHF is done on CPU
quiz.explanation: Pre-training learns weights from scratch by predicting the next token across trillions of tokens of raw internet text — this is the dominant compute cost. The result is a base model that is good at predicting text but does not follow instructions or have safety properties. RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) then fine-tunes the base model: human raters rank model outputs, a reward model learns to predict these rankings, and the LLM is updated via PPO to maximise reward model scores, producing an aligned assistant.

quiz.question: What is 'hallucination' in the context of LLMs, and why does it occur?
options: A visual glitch caused by running the model at high temperature settings
When the model generates plausible-sounding but factually incorrect information because it produces the most probable token sequence regardless of factual grounding
When the model refuses to answer a question due to safety filters
A deliberate feature that allows the model to generate creative fictional content
quiz.explanation: LLMs generate the most statistically probable continuation of a token sequence. When the correct answer is not well-represented in training data, the model still produces text — it generates something that looks superficially like a plausible answer. There is no internal fact-checker or mechanism to signal 'I don't know this' and refuse. Hallucination is worst for specific low-frequency facts (obscure statistics, names, citations) and is mitigated by RAG, which grounds the model's response in retrieved documents.

quiz.question: What does temperature control in LLM sampling, and what does temperature=0 produce?
options: It controls the context window size; temperature=0 uses no context
It scales logits before softmax, controlling distribution sharpness; temperature=0 produces greedy decoding, always selecting the highest-probability token
It sets the learning rate during fine-tuning; temperature=0 freezes weights
It controls the number of transformer layers activated; temperature=0 uses only the first layer
quiz.explanation: Temperature is a scalar applied to logits before the softmax: logits are divided by T. Low T (< 1) sharpens the distribution toward the highest-probability token, making output more deterministic and factual but also more repetitive. High T (> 1) flattens the distribution, increasing output variety and creativity. At T→0, the softmax approaches a one-hot distribution on the argmax — this is greedy decoding, always picking the single most likely token.

quiz.question: What are Chinchilla scaling laws, and what do they imply about how to train LLMs?
options: Laws derived from chinchilla fur patterns showing that model weights should be sparsified like animal fur
Empirical findings that for a fixed compute budget, training a smaller model on proportionally more tokens (roughly 20 tokens per parameter) outperforms training a larger model on fewer tokens
Rules governing how model size must scale with context window length
Guidelines requiring that all LLMs must be evaluated on a standard chinchilla benchmark dataset
quiz.explanation: The Chinchilla paper (Hoffmann et al., DeepMind 2022) showed that previous large models like GPT-3 were significantly undertrained. With a fixed compute budget, the optimal strategy is ~20 tokens per parameter: a 7B model should train on 140B tokens, not 300B tokens spread over a 175B model. LLaMA 3 deliberately over-trains (15 trillion tokens for 8B params) to produce a smaller model that is cheaper to run at inference while matching larger models trained optimally.

quiz.question: What is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and what problem does it solve?
options: A training technique that retrieves similar training examples to augment loss computation
An inference-time technique that retrieves relevant documents and injects them into the prompt, letting the model answer questions using current or private information not in its training weights
A method to increase the effective context window by compressing the KV-cache using retrieval
A hardware technique that retrieves model weights from secondary storage to reduce GPU memory usage
quiz.explanation: LLMs have a knowledge cutoff and cannot access information not in their training data. RAG addresses this: at inference time, the user query is embedded into a vector, similar document chunks are retrieved from a vector database (cosine similarity search), and those chunks are inserted into the prompt context. The model then generates its answer by reasoning over the retrieved documents rather than purely from parametric memory. This makes LLMs useful for private knowledge bases, up-to-date information, and reducing hallucination on factual questions.
